LONDON, England (CNN) — Pete Sampras, the former world number one, has declared newly crowned French Open champion Roger Federer the greatest player in the history of the sport.

The 37-year-old American, affectionately nicknamed "Pistol Pete" for his formidable serve, captured a then-record 14 Grand Slam singles titles over the course of his 15-year career, yet the French Open crown eluded him throughout. By defeating Sweden's Robin Soderling 6-1, 7-6, 6-4 in Sunday's final, Federer not only matched Sampras's storied record but also became just the sixth man in history to complete a career Grand Slam by winning all four major titles.

This achievement, according to Sampras, cements the 27-year-old Swiss star's legacy as the finest player ever to grace the sport. "What he's done over the past five years has never, ever been done — and probably will never happen again," Sampras told the Guardian. "Regardless of whether he won here or not, he goes down as the greatest ever. This just confirms it."

"I'm obviously delighted for Roger," Sampras added of the new champion and world number two, who had suffered defeat in three consecutive French Open finals at the hands of Spain's Rafael Nadal. "If anyone deserves this, it's Roger. He's come so close before."

Speaking exclusively to CNN following his victory, Federer expressed profound relief at having rebounded from a challenging 2008, during which he relinquished both his world number one ranking and his Australian Open and Wimbledon titles to Nadal.

"It's been a fantastic day — to finally secure that elusive French title is simply unbelievable," Federer said. "I always believed I had what it takes to win it, but actually holding the trophy, after everything I've been through, is beyond words. I couldn't be prouder in this moment.

"For me, retirement was never a question. I worked incredibly hard in the off-season. Losing in semifinals and finals was suddenly no longer good enough for people — but this victory has proven many doubters wrong, and the timing means everything."

The historic significance of the win was not lost on Federer himself. "These records mean a great deal to me, particularly over these last few years, as I've come to realize I belong among the greatest players of all time. I do enjoy breaking records, because I've always looked up to legends like Sampras, Agassi, Connors, and McEnroe — to be counted among them is truly special."

Yet in a pointed message to his rivals, the champion made clear his ambitions remain far from satisfied: "I still feel I have much more to give. I'm only 27, and I hope to compete for many more years and add many more titles to my collection."

Even his vanquished opponent offered high praise. "For me, he is the best there has ever been — and I should know, having played him many times," Soderling, ranked twelfth in the world, told CNN.

Federer's attention now turns to the year's third Grand Slam, Wimbledon, where he will seek to surpass Björn Borg's record by claiming a sixth title at the All England Club when play begins on June 22.

Federer's landmark achievement also drew recognition from International Olympic Committee President Jacques Rogge, who similarly hailed the Swiss as tennis's greatest-ever player. "Today I wrote to Roger Federer to congratulate him on this unique achievement, because I consider him the best player of all time," Rogge told reporters at a briefing in Brussels on Monday.

Rogge further revealed that his letter expressed hope that Federer would compete at the 2012 London Olympics — a fitting prospect, given that Federer already boasts an Olympic gold medal, won in men's doubles alongside compatriot Stanislas Wawrinka at the 2008 Beijing Games.

# London Simmers as Historic Heatwave Grips England

LONDON, England (CNN) — Residents and visitors across the British capital sought relief from unusually high temperatures this week as a prolonged heatwave settled over much of England, straining infrastructure and prompting health warnings from officials.

Temperatures in London climbed well above seasonal norms, with forecasters noting this could rank among the warmest periods recorded in the city in recent years. Parks across the capital, from Hyde Park to Hampstead Heath, filled with people seeking shade beneath trees or cooling off in fountains and ponds, while ice cream vendors reported some of their busiest days of the year.

The Greater London Authority issued heat-health alerts, urging residents—particularly the elderly and those with pre-existing health conditions—to stay hydrated, avoid strenuous activity during peak afternoon hours, and check on vulnerable neighbors. Hospitals across the city reported an uptick in heat-related admissions, though officials stressed that emergency services remained well-equipped to handle the surge.

Public transport also felt the strain. London's Underground system, much of which lacks air conditioning due to its age and tunnel design, saw temperatures inside carriages soar, prompting Transport for London to distribute water at major stations and remind commuters to carry bottles during their journeys.

Beyond the capital, the heatwave's effects rippled across England. Rail operators imposed speed restrictions on certain lines to prevent tracks from buckling in the extreme heat, while several outdoor events and festivals adjusted schedules to avoid the hottest parts of the day.

Climate scientists have pointed to the increasing frequency of such heatwaves as consistent with broader patterns linked to climate change, noting that what was once considered an anomaly is becoming a more regular feature of British summers.

As the mercury is expected to gradually decline over the coming days, officials continue to monitor conditions closely, with many Londoners hoping for a return to the country's more typically mild and unpredictable weather.

## Voices From Tennis History

The achievement prompted immediate reflection from across the sport, with legends weighing in on where Federer now stood.

**Rod Laver**, the only man to complete two calendar-year Grand Slams, offered high praise: "Roger has now done something very few players in the history of our sport have accomplished. To win all four majors, and to do it with the elegance and style he brings to the court — it puts him in rarefied air. I've always believed he's one of the greatest players I've seen."

**Björn Borg**, whose own career was defined by dominance at Roland Garros paired with heartbreak at Wimbledon, was blunt in his assessment: "This was the last big question mark for Roger. Now there is no argument. He is the complete champion. I never won the U.S. Open, so I understand what it means to have that one title elude you. For him to finally get Paris — it completes the picture."

**John McEnroe**, never shy with opinions, went further: "I've been saying for a while that he's the greatest we've ever seen, and this pretty much erases any doubt. The variety, the shots he can produce, and now he's proven he can win on every surface against every kind of opponent. Sampras never won the French. Borg never won the U.S. Open. Federer has now done it all."

**Andre Agassi**, who presented the trophy, reflected on the symbolism: "To hand him that trophy, knowing what this title represents — it's a special moment for the sport. Roger plays the game in a way that's timeless. This title makes his case as the greatest of all time very difficult to dispute."

Even **Rafael Nadal**, the man who had denied Federer in Paris on three previous occasions, offered gracious words from afar: "Roger deserves this. He has been the best player in the world for many years, and now he has won everywhere. Nobody can question his career anymore."

## A Historic Summer

The French Open triumph proved to be the opening act of a remarkable run. Weeks later, Federer defeated Andy Roddick in a marathon Wimbledon final, 16-14 in the fifth set, to claim his 15th Grand Slam title and surpass Sampras's record outright.

Sampras himself, watching his record fall, was characteristically measured: "Records are made to be broken. Roger is a phenomenal champion, and if anyone was going to break it, I'm glad it was someone who respects the game the way he does."

## Legacy Redefined

By the end of that summer, the conversation around Federer had fundamentally shifted. No longer was he merely a dominant player of his era — he had become, in the eyes of many historians and rivals alike, a serious candidate for the greatest of all time.

**Billie Jean King**, weighing in on the broader significance, noted: "What Roger has done is remind us what's possible when talent meets discipline meets opportunity. Completing the career Grand Slam is one of the hardest things to do in our sport, because it demands you master surfaces and conditions that are almost contradictory in what they require. He did that."

As Federer lifted the Coupe des Mousquetaires that afternoon in Paris, the tennis world watched a career narrative reach its resolution. The clay court that had haunted him for years had finally yielded — and with it, any remaining doubts about his place among the pantheon of the sport's all-time greats.
